analysis.one_liner: Allows foreign-built ships to carry goods between the mainland, Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and other U.S. islands, cutting shipping costs.
analysis.headline: Introduced with zero cosponsors, the bill was referred to committees and a subcommittee but never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law — the Jones Act — requires that ships moving goods between U.S. ports be built in the United States, mostly American-owned, and mostly American-crewed. Because U.S.-built and U.S.-operated ships cost far more to build and run, shipping goods to Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, Guam, and other island communities costs several times what the same shipment would cost on the open market. This bill would exempt that island trade from those requirements, letting foreign-built vessels carry the cargo, while applying international labor, safety, and environmental standards and keeping some U.S. crewing rules. Its sponsor argued this would lower the price of food, fuel, and everyday goods for island residents.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of Puerto Rico, Hawaii, Alaska, and other noncontiguous U.S. communities, who pay substantially higher prices for shipped goods because of the Jones Act; also retailers and importers in those places, who bear the freight costs that get passed on to shoppers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers in Hawaii, Puerto Rico, Alaska, Guam

how_it_helps.text: The bill exempts foreign-built, foreign-flagged freight vessels of at least 1,000 gross tons from the Jones Act's build-American and ownership requirements when carrying merchandise in noncontiguous trade — the routes between the mainland and places like Puerto Rico, Hawaii, Alaska, and Guam [S2][S3].

Foreign ships generally cost far less to build and operate than Jones Act-qualified vessels, so opening these routes to them would lower freight rates and, in turn, the retail price of shipped goods for island residents [S2].

The bill tries to blunt the downside for workers: it keeps U.S. crewing requirements for the exempted vessels 'to the extent required of vessels registered under section 12102,' sets minimum international labor standards for all vessels in the coastwise trade, and gives foreign employers' injured crew access to U.S. district courts and optional Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act coverage [S3].

It also requires all vessels in the coastwise trade, foreign or American, to meet U.S. and international environmental standards, and to comply with U.S. tax and environmental laws, with named agents for legal service [S3].

analysis.who_pays: U.S.-flag ocean carriers that hold a protected, higher-priced market on these routes (carriers like those serving Hawaii and Puerto Rico), and U.S. shipyards that depend on Jones Act demand for American-built ships, would lose sales and pricing power. Some U.S. merchant mariner jobs could be affected, though the bill retains partial U.S. crewing requirements.

drawbacks.text: Critics of Jones Act exemptions argue they erode the U.S. shipbuilding industrial base and the American merchant marine that the military relies on for sealift in a crisis — a national-security cost that is hard to reverse once the protected market is gone [S2].

The bill's labor and safety protections rest on 'recognized international standards' chosen by the Secretary of Transportation rather than the stricter U.S. standards Jones Act vessels must meet, so foreign-crewed ships could operate under weaker rules than American ones [S3].
The exemption applies only to freight vessels of 1,000 gross tons or more and only to noncontiguous routes, so smaller communities and feeder routes would see little or no benefit [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers in Puerto Rico, Hawaii, Alaska, and other island jurisdictions, the benefit is direct and well documented: they pay markedly higher shipping-inflated prices for everyday goods. The main costs fall on a concentrated industry — U.S. shipyards and Jones Act carriers — and on the merchant marine workforce, and the national-security argument against erosion of the shipbuilding base is serious but long-term. The bill attempts to address labor and environmental concerns but leaves standards in regulators' discretion. On balance, this is a targeted consumer-relief bill whose costs are real but borne mostly by a protected industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in December 2019 with no cosponsors, referred to two House committees and then a maritime subcommittee, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Ed Case (D-HI) introduced the bill on December 19, 2019, as a Jones Act exemption for noncontiguous trade [S1][S2][S5].

It was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the Education and Labor Committee, then to the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation on December 20, 2019; the record shows no further action for the rest of the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: U.S.-flag ocean carriers and domestic shipyards kept the Jones Act's legally protected market intact, so shipping rates — and prices for goods in Puerto Rico, Hawaii, and Alaska — stayed where they were.

for.name: Rep. Ed Case
for.role: U.S. Representative for Hawaii, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Noncontiguous Shipping Relief Act of 2019 and delivered introductory remarks supporting it.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over maritime law; never scheduled a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Subcommittee, where it sat without action for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: U.S.-flag ocean carriers and domestic shipbuilding industry
against.role: Jones Act beneficiaries serving Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico routes
against.what_they_did: Long-standing, well-documented opposition to Jones Act exemptions and repeals, which would open their protected routes to foreign competition.

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls occurred and the bill had no cosponsors, so no voting pattern exists; the sponsor was a Democrat from Hawaii, and Jones Act repeal efforts historically draw backers in both parties from island states while drawing opposition from maritime-industry districts in both parties.

industries.industry: U.S.-flag ocean shipping carriers (Jones Act trade)
industries.note: These carriers charge substantially higher freight rates on legally protected island routes; the exemption would let cheaper foreign vessels compete, cutting their revenue and pricing power. Their gain from the status quo is the public's higher cost of goods.

The Jones Act requires domestic-built ships for this trade, guaranteeing U.S. yards a captive market; exempting the routes removes that demand. The industry argues this also erodes national sealift capacity.

industries.industry: U.S. merchant marine (seafarers and maritime unions)
industries.note: Foreign crews on exempted vessels would displace some U.S. mariner jobs, though the bill retains partial U.S. crewing requirements and adds international labor standards and injury-liability protections for all coastwise crews.

industries.industry: Retailers and importers in Puerto Rico, Hawaii, Alaska, and island territories
industries.note: Lower freight costs cut their input costs, and those savings are the mechanism by which island consumers would see lower prices.
